newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani bank scandal inquiry absolves president.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani bank scandal inquiry absolves president.

text.p: A judicial inquiry into a banking scandal in Pakistan absolved President Farooq Leghari of any wrongdoing, a report released on Sunday said.
"It is the confirmed opinion of the commission, based on the evidence before it, that the allegations against the president are unfounded," a five-judge commission found unanimously.

In 1994 then opposition leader Nawaz Sharif accused Leghari of accepting money from Yunus Habib, former chief operating officer of the private Mehran Bank Ltd, via a land transaction involving anonymous buyers and fake accounts.
Leghari has repeatedly denied the charges.
The commission said the president had sold the land but at prices that did not exceed market rates. The transaction was done genuinely through the bank and was in his in name.
"No evidence whatsoever was led before the commission that the payment made for the land sold by President Farooq Leghari and his co-sharers was excessive and beyond the market rates."
Four of the judges said the families of Sharif and his political Ally Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain had taken loans from Habib without proper formalities or collateral.

"The two advances to Chaudhry Sugar Mills and Phalia Sugar Mills, whose directors/proprietors belonged to the Nawaz Sharif family and the Senator Chaudhry Shujaat Hussain family, was evidently to obtain political support and protection, as the members of the two families were important figures in the political party that constituted the government both at the centre and in Punjab (province)," the judges found.
However, the president of the commission, Judge Abdul Qadeer Chaudhry who has since retired, filed a minority opinion saying that Sharif and Hussain had not been given a hearing.

The same four judges absolved Aftab Sheao and Anwar Saifullah, both members of Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party, of charges that they had received money from the Mehran Bank. The commission president did not endorse that view.
The inquiry was set up in 1994 with a brief to investigate allegations that the bank had provided illegal gratification, loans and other benefits to government servants and politicians.
The inquiry concluded its work in 1995. It was not immediately clear why its publication had been delayed.
